extracted.intended_audience: cognitive neuroscientists, neuroimagers, psychologists and clinicians studying the neural mechanisms of humour
extracted.subtask_description: A literature-review style synthesis of neural, cognitive, developmental and clinical dimensions relevant to humour detection, comprehension and appreciation, with emphasis on neuroimaging findings and individual-difference moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core neural network for humour processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour seems to engage a core network of cortical and subcortical structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review identifies temporo‑occipito‑parietal areas together with mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic structures and the amygdala as the core network involved in humour processing (see abstract and multiple cited neuroimaging studies). Use this network as the primary target when interpreting humour-related brain activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity detection and resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporo‑occipito‑parietal areas are involved in detecting and resolving incongruity (mismatch between expected and presented stimuli).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many studies treat detection/resolution of incongruity as the cognitive kernel of humour (applies to cartoons, verbal jokes, and other stimuli). Experimental paradigms should operationalize and separate incongruity detection from its resolution to map associated activations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward and salience processing (mesocorticolimbic system and amygdala)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic system and the amygdala are key structures for reward and salience processing during humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activity in mesolimbic/reward regions is commonly interpreted as humour appreciation/reward; amygdala activity indexes salience/relevance. Studies measuring appreciation should include measures (behavioral/subjective) that correlate with reward-region activation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation of cognitive versus affective components
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour processing comprises separable cognitive (comprehension, incongruity-resolution, theory-of-mind) and affective (appreciation, reward) components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs and analyses should attempt to dissociate comprehension/detection from affective appreciation (e.g., separate tasks or contrasts), following work that 'segregates cognitive and affective components' (Goel & Dolan; Chan et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate detection (getting it) from appreciation (finding it funny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neural correlates differ between humour detection/comprehension and humour appreciation/enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use behavioral indices (accuracy, reaction time, subjective amusement ratings) alongside imaging contrasts to distinguish neural signatures of 'getting' a joke from the hedonic response to it (cites: Coulson & Kutas; Moran et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Task and stimulus modality matters (verbal vs nonverbal, sight gags, films, stand-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different stimuli (verbal jokes, nonverbal cartoons, sight gags, comic films, stand‑up) elicit distinct neural responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stimulus modality intentionally and interpret activations in light of modality-specific processing (e.g., language areas for verbal jokes, visuospatial areas for sight gags). Several cited studies compare modalities (Watson et al.; Franklin & Adams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appropriate neuroimaging methods and cross-method comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour research employs fMRI, PET, NIRS (including hyperscanning) and meta-analytic approaches; measurement choice affects findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review references fMRI, PET and NIRS studies and a quantitative comparison of NIRS and fMRI; researchers should match method to hypotheses (temporal vs spatial resolution) and consider method-specific limitations when integrating results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric modulation and meta-analysis as analytic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Parametric modulation of humour and meta-analytic summaries are useful for mapping humour-related activations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures and cited work use meta-analysis of activations and parametric modulation contrasts; apply parametric designs to capture graded humour intensity and use meta-analysis to synthesize heterogeneous paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider individual differences (personality, temperament, age, IQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personality traits, temperament, age and IQ influence neural responses to humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies should measure and control for individual-difference variables (e.g., trait cheerfulness, temperament, IQ) because they modulate reward/emotion-region activity and humour appreciation (cites: Mobbs et al.; Vrticka et al.; Samson et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine sex/gender differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex differences modulate brain activation during humour appreciation and processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sex as a factor or report sex-disaggregated results; several studies find gender differences in neural correlates and processing modes (Azim et al.; Kohn et al.; Vrticka et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include clinical and developmental populations where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour processing is altered in clinical (schizophrenia, autism, narcolepsy, depression, cataplexy) and developmental contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand mechanisms and translational relevance, examine patient groups and developmental samples; the review cites multiple studies documenting deficits or altered activations in these populations and highlights therapeutic/clinical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-of-mind and right temporoparietal junction involvement (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks invoking mental-state inference recruit temporoparietal regions, but right TPJ activity may not be selective for theory-of-mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing activations to mentalizing, interpret rTPJ findings cautiously and consider control tasks, as some literature (Mitchell 2008) questions selectivity; separate mentalizing from attention/salience functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive function and mentalizing contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive functions and mentalizing abilities contribute to humour generation and appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess executive function and mentalizing when studying humour (e.g., in depression or social anxiety), since these cognitive capacities correlate with humour processing performance and neural responses (Uekermann et al.; Marjoram et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic ambiguity, puns and linguistic ambiguity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic ambiguity and puns engage specific neural mechanisms linking humour to semantic processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include manipulations of ambiguity (puns vs unambiguous jokes) to probe language-semantic contributions to humour; Bekinschtein et al. show links between humour and semantic ambiguity processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social context and expressive regulation modulate humour perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Social regulation (e.g., expressive suppression) and contextual cues alter humour perception and its neural correlates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for social/contextual factors and emotion-regulation strategies in experimental designs; studies show humour perception differs with/without expressive suppression and is socially regulated (Korb et al.; Goel & Dolan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate neural correlates of laughter versus humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and humour have overlapping but distinct neural correlates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying physiological/behavioral outcomes (e.g., laughter, smiling) versus subjective humour experience, distinguish the neural signatures of expressive components from those of cognitive/affective humour processing (Wild et al.; studies on mirth and physiological effects).
